items.question: What is EmDash?
items.answer: EmDash is an Astro-native CMS with a full admin panel. You model content in the admin, and your Astro site queries it. It deploys to Cloudflare Workers or to a Node.js server.

items.question: Do I need Cloudflare to run EmDash?
items.answer: No. Cloudflare Workers with D1 and R2 is one option. EmDash also runs on Node.js with SQLite and local file storage, for example on a VPS. The EmDash review on bitdoze.com compares both.

items.question: Are the themes and plugins listed here free?
items.answer: Each listing carries a Free or Paid badge. Paid entries show the price and link to the seller's page.

items.question: Who runs this site?
items.answer: I'm Dragos. I write the guides at bitdoze.com and publish the videos on the Bitdoze YouTube channel.

The plugin never talks to an email service itself; it calls ctx.email.send(), so it works with both options and any future provider.

data.title: Stop contact form spam with Cloudflare Turnstile
data.excerpt: The contact form on this site was feeding the inbox junk. Turnstile took it to zero: the real pipeline, the exact fields a bot must fake, verified curl tests, and the cache trap we hit.

$media.alt: A paper mailbox behind a small turnstile gate, letters held at the checkpoint

children.text: The contact form on this site runs exactly the setup below. Before Turnstile it was collecting scripted submissions - the built-in filters caught some, but enough got through to make the inbox a chore. After adding it, junk posts stopped creating rows entirely: what lands in the inbox now is real people and nothing else.

The short version: the Contact Forms plugin renders a Cloudflare Turnstile widget on the form, the browser hands back a token, and the submit route verifies that token with Cloudflare before it stores anything or sends mail. A POST without a valid token gets a 303 redirect to cf_status=challenge - no database row, no email. Everything below is the real pipeline from the plugin source, plus tests I ran against the live form.

body.caption: The submit pipeline: the honeypot and fill-time traps run first and lie to the bot, Turnstile verifies the token at the door, and only then does anything reach the inbox.

image.alt: The submission pipeline: envelope, honey pot, clock and turnstile gate guarding the inbox

children.text: What you need

items.text: A Cloudflare account (the free plan covers Turnstile)
Contact Forms plugin 1.1.0 or newer
Two keys from the dashboard: the site key and the secret key
About fifteen minutes

children.text: How a submission is judged
Every POST to the submit route passes these gates, in this order. The order matters: a request can only fail one gate, and which one tells you what the sender was.

items.title: Honeypot
items.body: The cf_hp field is invisible to humans and bots fill it. Tripping it returns a fake cf_status=sent and stores nothing - the bot thinks it won.

items.title: Form lookup
items.body: cf_slug must match an enabled form. No match means cf_status=error before anything else is checked.

items.title: Minimum fill time
items.body: The hidden cf_ts field carries the page-load timestamp. A submit under 1.5 seconds old is a bot and gets another fake sent.

items.title: Turnstile verify
items.body: When both keys are set, cf-turnstile-response goes to Cloudflare siteverify with the secret key and the visitor IP. Missing or rejected token: cf_status=challenge.

items.title: Rate limit
items.body: Counts stored submissions from the same IP in the last hour against the configured cap, 20 by default. Over it: cf_status=rate_limited.

items.title: Field validation
items.body: Each field is checked against the form definition. Failures return cf_status=invalid with the bad keys echoed in cf_fields.

items.title: Store
items.body: The row is written first - before email - so a mail outage never loses a message. That is why a broken mail config shows status saved, not sent.

items.title: Email
items.body: The notification goes through the site's configured provider, and the row records the attempt. If the form has send confirmation on, the visitor gets an auto-reply too.

children.text: The honeypot and fill-time traps return a success-shaped redirect instead of an error. A scraper watching responses cannot tell which gate caught it, so it never learns what to fix. You can watch this happen yourself in the curl tests below.
The two contracts
Everything the route needs is in the posted form data. These are the real field names - the prefix matters, and getting it wrong is the first trap:

items.label: cf_slug
items.value: The form slug to submit to. Plain "slug" is ignored and returns error

items.label: cf_hp
items.value: Honeypot. Must be empty; the input is hidden and never filled by humans

items.label: cf_ts
items.value: Page-load timestamp in ms; posts younger than 1.5 s are bots

items.label: cf-turnstile-response
items.value: The token Cloudflare's widget writes into the form

items.label: cf_page
items.value: Optional URL the submit came from, stored on the row

items.label: your fields
items.value: Whatever the form defines - name, email, subject, message here

children.text: The answer is never JSON. The route 303-redirects back to the referring page with cf_status in the query string, so a plain HTML form with no JavaScript still completes the loop - the browser just lands on a page that can read the status.
Set it up

items.title: Create a Turnstile site
items.body: In the Cloudflare dashboard, open Turnstile and choose Add site. Enter your real hostname and keep the Managed widget mode. Cloudflare shows the site key and secret key once; copy both.

items.title: Open the plugin settings
items.body: Admin → Plugins → Contact forms → Settings. The two Turnstile fields only exist on 1.1.0 and newer.

items.title: Paste both keys and save
items.body: The site key renders the widget; the secret key verifies tokens. Set only one and the gate stays off: a half-configured pair is treated as unconfigured, not half-on.

items.title: Redeploy or purge the cache
items.body: If pages are cached, the cached HTML has no widget on it. Cached pages keep collecting challenge failures until the cache refreshes.

items.title: Test it
items.body: Load the form page, confirm the widget, submit once yourself for the happy path, then run the curl below for the bot path.

body.caption: The plugin settings screen: the Turnstile site key and secret key sit next to the built-in rate limit.

image.alt: The contact forms plugin settings page showing the Turnstile key fields

children.text: Test it from the outside
These are real responses from this site's live endpoint, not a mock. A tokenless POST must be challenged:

No row is written, no mail goes out. Now the trap I fell into writing this: my first test posted slug=contact instead of cf_slug=contact and got cf_status=error - the route read an empty slug and reported the form missing, which is honest but misleading when you typo the field name. If you see error instead of challenge, check the field names before the keys.

That sent is a lie in the good direction: the response says success, the database got nothing. The submissions inbox on this site held eight rows when I checked - all real, every one with an email status recorded.
What the status codes mean

items.label: sent
items.value: Stored and emailed - or a fake success fed to the honeypot and time traps

items.label: saved
items.value: Stored, but the notification email failed; the row keeps the error

items.label: challenge
items.value: Turnstile token missing or rejected; nothing was stored

items.label: rate_limited
items.value: The hourly per-IP cap tripped

items.label: invalid
items.value: Fields failed validation; the bad keys echo back in cf_fields

items.label: error
items.value: Form slug unknown or disabled - or too many posted fields

body.caption: Submissions that pass land in the inbox with an email status for each one. Blocked posts never get a row.

image.alt: The submissions inbox listing stored form entries with status and email columns

children.text: What a stored row contains
Each passing submission records more than the answers - enough to debug delivery problems later without a second system:

items.text: The answers plus the field labels at submit time
IP, user agent and country (from the edge request)
The page URL the submit came from
emailStatus and emailAttempts, so a provider outage is visible, not silent
A new / read / flagged state you can triage in the inbox

children.text: The fail-open trade-off, honestly

When Turnstile is configured but siteverify cannot be reached, the plugin accepts the submission. The reasoning: a Cloudflare outage should never take your contact form down with it. The cost: a silently broken verifier quietly turns the spam check off - you find out via a spam spike, not an error. If junk suddenly reappears, suspect the keys before the bots got smarter.

body.title: The cache trap we actually hit

children.text: Keys were saved, but the page showed no widget. The deploy had warmed a widget-less copy of the contact page into the Workers cache and kept serving it. A redeploy fixed it. If the widget does not appear after saving, suspect the cache before the keys.
Tuning it afterwards

items.text: Rate limit per IP per hour: 20 by default, accepts 1 to 1000; the count is over stored rows, so challenged posts do not eat the budget
Keep submissions for (days): 0 keeps everything forever
Confirmation email: each form can auto-reply to the visitor's email field - the contact form here has it on
Extra debug: plugin settings has a switch that turns on verbose submit logs
Submissions export to CSV from the admin inbox when you need them out

children.text: Worth knowing

items.label: Price
items.value: Free with any Cloudflare account

items.label: User friction
items.value: Usually invisible; Managed mode only challenges suspects

items.label: Privacy
items.value: No tracking cookies, no puzzle farm

items.label: Mode used here
items.value: Managed

items.title: Does it stop all spam?
items.body: It stops automated posts and most scripted junk. A determined human can still pass a challenge. Flagged submissions can be quarantined in the inbox: stored as spam, never emailed.

items.title: Does it work without JavaScript?
items.body: The widget needs JavaScript in the browser. That is the point: bots posting the raw endpoint get challenged regardless.

items.title: What if Cloudflare is down?
items.body: Verification fails open: submissions are accepted so the form never goes offline with them. Watch for a spam spike as the telltale.

items.title: Where do real submissions go?
items.body: The admin inbox under Plugins → Contact forms, plus an email through the site's configured provider.

body.caption: The live form on this site: in managed mode the widget renders nothing until Cloudflare decides a visitor needs a challenge.

image.alt: The public contact form rendered on the site

items.text: The widget renders on the form page
A tokenless POST gets cf_status=challenge
A filled honeypot gets a fake sent and stores nothing
A real submit is stored and emailed
A quiet inbox for a week

data.title: Nineteen content widgets for EmDash posts and pages
data.excerpt: Callouts, numbered steps, tabs, code blocks, video facades and more for the block editor. What ships in the plugin, how to install it, and where to see it working.

$media.alt: A grid of small paper widget cards, accordion folds, checklists, buttons, laid out like letterpress blocks

children.text: Articles on this site needed more than paragraphs. Callouts for warnings, numbered steps for walkthroughs, code blocks for commands, a table of contents on long posts. The stock block editor ships a lean set on purpose, so I built the Content Widgets plugin: nineteen block types for the EmDash editor, usable in post bodies and on regular pages.

The short version: install @bitdoze.com/emdashhq-widgets from the registry, allow the widget types on your blocks field, copy the renderers from the package's site/ folder into your project, and the editor's slash menu grows nineteen new entries. Everything renders on the server, picks up the site's type scale and colors through CSS variables, and ships no client-side bundle.

body.caption: The catalog page the plugin adds under Plugins → Content Widgets: every block with a preview, a one-line description and its type name.

image.alt: The Content Widgets catalog in the EmDash admin

children.text: What actually ships
Nineteen blocks is a lot of names. Grouped by the job they do:

items.text: Prose: Portable Text paragraphs between the widgets
Notice: info, success, warning and danger callouts for gotchas
Checklist and steps: task lists and numbered walkthroughs
Accordion and tabs: collapsed sections and side-by-side variants
Divider: a styled rule between sections
Image: figure with caption, served through the media pipeline
Code: syntax highlighting with filename and language label
YouTube: a click-to-load facade, privacy-enhanced host
Embed: a sandboxed iframe for anything else
Button: links with twelve built-in icons
Cards: small link grids for related reading
Quote: pull quotes with attribution
Facts: a label/value fact sheet for specs and pricing
Product: a review box with rating, pros/cons and an affiliate disclosure line
Table of contents: built from the post's own headings
Series: previous/next navigation for multi-part posts
Latest posts: a recent-articles list that skips the current post

children.text: What the editor actually stores
This is a real notice block lifted from the demo post's stored body - the whole record, nothing trimmed:

Three details matter. The _type is the contract between editor and renderer; _version versions the shape so a plugin update can migrate old blocks; and _key is immutable - the API rejects an update that reuses a key with a different type, which is worth knowing the first time you rewrite a body through the REST API. Rich text fields like body carry real Portable Text, so spans, marks and links survive intact.
Install it

items.label: From the registry
items.body: Admin → Plugins → Browse → find Content Widgets → Install. The package is @bitdoze.com/emdashhq-widgets on plugins.emdashcms.com. This is the path for most sites: the registry handles versions and updates.

items.label: From source
items.body: Clone the plugin into your site's plugins/ directory, register it under sandboxed: in astro.config.mjs, and add it to package.json as a file: dependency. Take this path when you want to edit the widgets themselves.

children.text: Allow the block types

New block types do not appear in the editor until a blocks field allows them. Open the collection, edit the blocks field, and tick the widget types under allowed types. In a seed file it looks like this:
Wire the renderers

Sandboxed plugins run in a Worker isolate and cannot register Astro components into a site's render pipeline. So the package ships its renderers as plain Astro files in site/ - you copy them into your project and they become your components, free of the sandbox. It is the distribution format, not a workaround.
Two ways to render them. Spread the shipped component map into your existing block renderer, or drop the standalone WidgetBlocks component on a widget-only field like a post body:

body.caption: Once the types are allowed, they show up in the block picker alongside the regular blocks.

image.alt: A widget block picked from the EmDash post editor

children.text: Anatomy of one widget

Every renderer is the same small shape - props carry the stored block value, markup is plain HTML, and styling reads theme tokens instead of hardcoding colors. Skinned down to its skeleton, a widget looks like this:

The wgt- class prefix keeps widget CSS from colliding with the theme, and var() tokens mean the same file renders correctly in a cream-paper theme or an ink-dark one. Copy a component, change the fields, and you have a custom widget that stores Portable Text like the built-ins.
Pages get them too

Nothing here is post-specific. The contact page's form block and this site's marketing pages use the same mechanism: any blocks field on any collection can allow the widget types, and the same WidgetBlocks component renders them. Write the field once, use the widgets everywhere.
See it working

Every block on the list is rendering in the demo post linked below, the same one you can open in this site's editor to inspect how it was put together - including the affiliate product card, which got a layout fix and an affiliate-card restyle in 1.0.3.

data.title: How the blog on this site works
data.excerpt: A posts collection, one Astro route and a hub block. The whole thing took an afternoon, including one redirect bug worth a warning.

$media.alt: A vintage printing press feeding out a magazine page, a stack of paper beside it

children.text: This site has a blog now. Not a separate app: a posts collection, one Astro route, and a block that lists articles on the /blog page. Here is the anatomy of it - real code, not pseudocode - so you can build the same thing, or take it apart to see how EmDash pieces fit together.

The short version: entries in a posts collection become routable via a urlPattern, one dynamic route renders each slug, a hub block lists them on a page, and cache tags make publish invalidate exactly the pages that show the post. Everything below is the actual implementation on this site.

items.label: Collection
items.value: posts: title, excerpt, cover, body blocks

items.label: Route
items.value: src/pages/blog/[slug].astro

items.label: Hub page
items.value: /blog, a page with a site_posts block

items.label: Rendering
items.value: Server-rendered on every request

items.label: Extras
items.value: Drafts, revisions, per-post SEO, sitemap, RSS

body.caption: The whole blog in three pieces: the posts collection holds the data, one route renders every slug, and the body blocks become the article.

image.alt: The blog pipeline: posts collection, one route, the rendered article

children.text: The collection

The posts collection is regular EmDash schema. The interesting bits are the urlPattern, which makes entries routable and lands them in the sitemap, and the body field, a blocks field where all the widgets live.
Two fields carry the listing pages: excerpt is the card text and meta description fallback, cover is the card image and og:image. Skip them and every surface downstream looks unfinished.
The route, annotated
One file renders every post. This is its real core - the redirects, the lookup, the cache tag, and the SEO resolution:

Four things worth stealing. The early 301s normalize the URL before any data work happens. The entry read runs in parallel with the site chrome read - one round trip, not two. A failed query sets no cache and returns a deliberately uncached 503 rather than a poisoned 500. And a missing post rewrites to the 404 page instead of rendering an empty shell.

The reading time on the post header is also computed, not stored: the route filters body blocks down to widget_prose, runs extractPlainText over their Portable Text, and divides the word count by 200. Every article's minutes stay honest automatically.
What the head gets

getSeoMeta resolves the SEO tab on each post - meta title, description, og image - and falls back to the title and excerpt when the fields are empty. Canonical and robots come along for free, and the cover doubles as og:image. Fill the SEO tab once and every surface agrees.
Why cacheHint matters

Passing the query's cacheHint to Astro.cache tags the response with the entries it read. Publishing a post then invalidates exactly the cached pages that show it: the article, /blog, and the homepage section. Skip the tag and edits wait out the cache lifetime. The same trick runs site-wide - the middleware tags public pages with site-scripts so changing analytics settings busts every page at once.
The hub page

/blog itself is an ordinary page with a site_posts block on it. The block queries the posts collection, orders by published date, and renders the newest article as a lead card with the rest in a grid. The page is content, not code: editors can move it, rename it and add blocks around it without touching the repo.
The same block with a limit of three is the "Latest from the blog" section on the homepage. One component, two placements, no duplicated markup.
The feed, annotated
rss.xml.ts builds one feed out of four collections. The whole trick is a small table - each collection declares which field holds its outbound link:

Tutorials link out to bitdoze.com, videos to YouTube, resources to npm or the registry - and posts get the internal /blog/ path as the special case. Each collection read also passes its own cacheHint, so publishing anything refreshes the feed too.
Drafts and publishing

Saving a post writes a draft revision; the live page only changes when you hit publish. That is why a saved-but-unpublished edit can look lost on the site while being perfectly visible in the admin - and why the REST API answers a PUT with a new revision id rather than a changed page. The SEO tab sits on the same editor screen, so meta title and description are part of the publish checklist rather than an afterthought.
Two traps worth knowing

Setting Astro's trailingSlash to "always" 404s every /_emdash/api/ route without a trailing slash; it briefly broke the contact form on this site. The sitemap emits slashless post URLs that 301 to the canonical form. That redirect is expected and harmless: do not try to fix it with trailingSlash.
Rewriting a post body through the API fails if a reused _key changes _type between revisions. Fresh keys per rewrite - the content update script rotates a key prefix for exactly this reason.
